Chapter 4: The Impact of White Supremacy on All Bodies
When you hear about racism, it’s easy to imagine it only hurts the people directly targeted by it. But honestly, the truth is a lot more complicated. White supremacy—the belief that White people are somehow better than others—ends up hurting everyone, just in different ways. Its effects don’t just show up in laws or institutions. They show up in our bodies, in families, and in communities, rippling out in ways that can be hard to see.
For many Black Americans, the impact is painfully obvious: there’s fear, anger, exhaustion, and that constant need to stay on guard. But here’s something we don’t talk about enough—White Americans are shaped by this system, too. Some learn to look away from others’ pain, almost numbing themselves to suffering. Others feel a heavy guilt or shame, never quite sure how to respond. And then there are those who get defensive, clinging to the idea that they’ve done nothing wrong.
These reactions aren’t just thoughts bouncing around in your head—they’re physical. Imagine a White person feeling threatened during a tough conversation about race. Suddenly, their heart starts racing, muscles tense up, breathing gets faster. Maybe they lash out, maybe they shut down or just want to disappear. It’s the body’s way of handling discomfort, trying to shield itself from pain.
And what about police officers? They’re often seen as the face of the system, but most of them start out wanting to do good. Pretty quickly, though, they learn to see danger everywhere. Their bodies get stuck in high alert, their minds wired to react in a split second. Over time, that takes a real toll. Some become hardened, some just go numb. Many find it tough to connect with their own families, unable to switch off those alarm bells their bodies have learned to ring.
The thing is, white supremacy’s effects are everywhere, but most of the time, they’re invisible. People don’t always notice how their bodies react to difference, to conflict, or to not knowing what’ll happen next. They don’t see how old patterns—passed down from generation to generation, reinforced by society—are shaping their reactions. But the body remembers, even when the mind tries to pretend it’s forgotten.
Healing starts by facing these truths, even when it’s uncomfortable. That means paying attention to how white supremacy shows up in everyday life—in what people say, how they move, how they react to each other. It means learning to sit with that discomfort, to really listen to what your body’s telling you, and to respond with care instead of defensiveness.
I want to share a story. There was a man who grew up in a family where race just wasn’t discussed. Whenever someone brought up the topic, he’d get anxious—his jaw would tighten, his breath would get shallow, and his mind would scramble for the right words. At first, he tried to push those feelings away. But over time, he learned to pause, to breathe, to allow himself to feel uncomfortable. Slowly, he opened up, became more willing to listen, and started connecting more deeply with others.
That’s what healing looks like. Not just for one person, but for whole communities. It’s about creating spaces where people can be honest about their pain, where bodies can finally relax, and where old wounds can start to heal. It’s about recognizing that white supremacy affects all of us, and that each of us has a role to play in the process.
The road to healing is slow, and it takes real courage. It means facing not just your own pain, but the pain carried by generations—and the pain carried by a whole nation. But if you can learn to sit with discomfort, to trust your body’s wisdom, and to believe that healing is possible, even when wounds run deep—you’re already taking the first step.
